explanations.answer: Pray at all times and not lose heart
explanations.explanation: Luke tells us Jesus spoke this parable “…about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart…” (Luke 18:1). The point comes first, before a single character walks on stage. Keep praying, baker, and keep your heart in it.

explanations.answer: Give to the poor and not grow weary
explanations.explanation: Giving to the poor is a good thing, but that's not what this verse says. Luke 18:1 says the parable is about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart. "Grow weary" sounds close, I know. But the verse is about praying, and about not losing heart while you do it.

explanations.answer: Keep watch and not fall asleep
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like it could belong to some other teaching, but it isn't the one here. Luke 18:1 says Jesus told this parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart. I once tried to keep watch over a batch and woke up face down next to the timer. Praying and not losing heart is the point of this one.
Not quite, friend. Luke 18:4 says "For a while he refused…" Only later did he say to himself that he would give her justice. So the answer is False, because the first ask didn't get her anywhere.
That's it. The text says "For a while he refused, but later he said to himself…" (Luke 18:4). So the widow didn't win on her first try. She kept appealing to him, and the judge's mind changed later.

Yes, pestering. The judge says it himself: "…because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice." (Luke 18:5). He doesn't say he suddenly cared. She kept coming, and he decided to give her justice.

The widow never threatens him in this parable. She keeps appealing to him, asking for justice against her adversary. The judge's own word in Luke 18:5 is "pestering." Asking again and again is a very different thing from a threat.

Nice try, but nobody in this story is sweet-talking the judge. He says she keeps pestering him, and that she will "…wear me out with her perpetual requests." (Luke 18:5). Nothing in the verse says she praised him. She just kept asking.
Day and night, baker. Jesus asks, "Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?" (Luke 18:7). That's no once-in-a-while cry. It keeps going, morning and midnight.

Once a year would be a pretty quiet cry. Jesus says His elect "…cry out to Him day and night?" (Luke 18:7). That's a whole lot more often than a yearly visit. Nobody here is on a yearly schedule, not even me with my oven cleaning.
Close to a regular rhythm, but Jesus says something different. He says His elect "…cry out to Him day and night?" (Luke 18:7). Every Sabbath isn't the phrase He uses. The phrase is day and night.
Promptly is the word. Jesus says, "I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf." (Luke 18:8). He asks first whether God will delay in helping them. Then He answers: promptly.

Eventually has a slow, shrugging feel, and that's not the word Jesus uses. He asks, "Will He delay in helping them?" and then says God "…will promptly carry out justice…" (Luke 18:7-8). Promptly means quick. Eventually is how some folks answer their group chats.
Reluctantly belongs to the judge's story, not to what Jesus says about God. The text gives no word like that for God. Jesus says He "…will promptly carry out justice on their behalf." (Luke 18:8).

True. Jesus closes with a question: "Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?" (Luke 18:8). "…Son of Man…" is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). I don't know when that day is, and Matthew 24:36 says only the Father does. That's why my ovens stay ready.

It's True. The last words of this part of the parable are a question: "Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?" (Luke 18:8). Jesus uses "…Son of Man…" as the name for Himself (Mark 2:10). So He ends by asking about faith, and the teaching isn't over yet.

Righteousness is right. Jesus told this parable “To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt…” (Luke 18:9). Those two things come together in the same sentence. I'm listening closely, baker.
Riches would make a different parable. Luke 18:9 says these people "…trusted in their own righteousness…" The trouble wasn't their bank accounts. It was where they placed their trust.

Strength is a good guess, but it isn't in the verse. Jesus speaks "To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt…" (Luke 18:9). The word is righteousness. They trusted in themselves as righteous.

A tax collector. The text says, "Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector." (Luke 18:10). Two men, one temple, and two very different prayers on the way.
A priest would fit at a temple, I'll give you that. But Luke 18:10 names the second man differently: "One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector." The parable never brings a priest on stage.
No sheep in this parable, friend. Luke 18:10 says, "One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector." Those are the two men who went up to pray. A shepherd isn't one of them.

explanations.answer: That he is not like other men
explanations.explanation: That's what he says: “God, I thank You that I am not like other men…” (Luke 18:11). He starts with thanks, but the thanks is about how he compares to everybody else. He even brings up the tax collector, saying “…or even like this tax collector.” (Luke 18:11). I'd call that a thank-you with a side-eye.
Forgiveness never comes up in his prayer. He thanks God "…that I am not like other men…" (Luke 18:11). He goes on to tell God about himself, not about his sins. That's why this answer doesn't match.
He doesn't thank God for listening. What he thanks God for is "…that I am not like other men…" (Luke 18:11). His prayer is mostly about himself and how he compares.

It's False, friend. After comparing himself to others, the Pharisee says, "I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire." (Luke 18:12). He talks about what he does, and there's no confession of sin in his prayer.
That's right. His next words are, "I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire." (Luke 18:12). He tells God what he does. He doesn't confess a single sin.

explanations.answer: God have mercy on me a sinner
explanations.explanation: Yes. He prays, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13). Eyes down, hand on his chest, and one short, honest sentence. I think the shortest prayer in the story is the one that says the most.

explanations.answer: God I have done my very best
explanations.explanation: That sounds more like the Pharisee's prayer, where he tells God what he does. The tax collector says something else: "God, have mercy on me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13). He doesn't talk about his best at all. He asks for mercy.

explanations.answer: God I am better than that man
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like the Pharisee, who prayed about being unlike "…this tax collector." (Luke 18:11). The tax collector says nothing like it. He stands at a distance and prays, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13).

True. Jesus says, "I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified." (Luke 18:14). The man who beat his breast and asked for mercy is the one who went home justified. That's the twist, and Jesus Himself gives it.

It's True. Jesus says, "I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified." (Luke 18:14). "This man" is the tax collector. The Pharisee, with all his fasting and tithing, is the one who is passed over.

Exalted. Jesus says, "For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted." (Luke 18:14). Lift yourself up and you get brought down. Stay low, and you get lifted. I learned that from a drawer, friend.

Forgotten isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "…the one who humbles himself will be exalted." (Luke 18:14). Humbling yourself isn't a path to being overlooked. The promise is that you'll be lifted up.

Judged isn't what Jesus says. He says, "…the one who humbles himself will be exalted." (Luke 18:14). Exalted means lifted up, and that's the word for the humble. It's the opposite of being humbled, which is what happens to the one who exalts himself.
